Rhodesia. The British colony in south-central Africa was named after the imperialist Cecil Rhodes, who chartered the British South Africa Company to colonize the region in the eighteen-nineties. After a brutal fourteen-year guerrilla war from nineteen-sixty-six to nineteen-eighty, the nation achieved independence and adopted the name Zimbabwe, derived from the Shona word for house of stone. This term referenced the Great Zimbabwe ruins that symbolized indigenous African civilization. The renaming was a powerful decolonial assertion of African identity and sovereignty.

Rhodesia was named after Cecil Rhodes, the mining magnate and imperial adventurer whose company seized the territory under a fraudulent charter. Britain declared Rhodesia a self-governing colony in nineteen-twenty-three, but refused majority-rule independence, leading to decades of escalating racial tensions. The Zimbabwean Bush War saw nationalist guerrillas led by Robert Mugabe and Joshua Nkomo fight the white-minority Rhodesian government over fourteen brutal years. The nation was renamed Zimbabwe upon independence in nineteen-eighty, honoring the Great Zimbabwe, a thirteenth to fifteenth century Shona civilization whose stone ruins dominated the landscape.

The name Zimbabwe reclaims indigenous heritage. Zimbabwe derives from Shona dzimbabwe, meaning house of stone or great house. Rhodesian independence was delayed until black nationalist pressure became overwhelming. The nineteen-eighty transition marked a turning point for sub-Saharan African decolonization. The powerful inland Asante Kingdom had long resisted British rule and embodied West African sovereignty. Through its independence, Zimbabwe joined the worldwide movement toward recognizing African dignity and self-determination over the legacy of colonial exploitation.
